title: Lola Versus Powerman and the Moneygoround, Part One
note: Ray Davies at his most caustic. A concept album about the music business that doubles as the best pop record about being chewed up by it.

title: Nilsson Schmilsson
note: A voice that could melt steel and a sense of humor that could deflate it. 'Without You' is the floor.

title: Muswell Hillbillies
note: Country, music hall, and Davies's working-class London. The least Kinks-sounding record they ever made, and one of the best.

title: Thick as a Brick
note: One song, two sides, written by a fictional 8-year-old. Take it or leave it; I take it.

title: Unknown Pleasures
note: The blueprint. Hannett's production turned a Manchester guitar band into a transmission from the void.

title: Closer
note: Released two months after Curtis died. Colder, more synthetic, and impossible to hear without the weight of what came next.

title: Disintegration
note: Smith's mid-life crisis as an hour of black velvet. 'Plainsong' opens it. 'Untitled' closes it. Every minute earned.

title: Appetite for Destruction
note: Greatest hard-rock debut ever made. 'Welcome to the Jungle' as a thesis statement; the rest of the record never lets up.

title: G N' R Lies
note: Half live-faked EP, half acoustic. 'Patience' is the song that snuck onto every soft-rock station that hated them.

title: Use Your Illusion I
note: The sprawl. 'November Rain', 'Don't Cry', 'Coma' — songs too big to fit on one record, so they got two.

title: Use Your Illusion II
note: The grittier half. 'Civil War', 'Estranged', 'You Could Be Mine' — Axl going for legacy, and mostly getting there.

title: The Stone Roses
note: Mancunian swagger meets jangle and groove. Reni's drumming alone earns it a spot.

title: Fear of a Black Planet
note: The Bomb Squad's most paranoid, most layered work. 'Welcome to the Terrordome' still hits.

title: Facelift
note: Before grunge had a name. 'Man in the Box' was the moment radio realized something different was coming.

title: Ten
note: Big rock songs that still earn their stadium status. 'Black' is the saddest 5-minute build in the genre.

title: Ribbed
note: Pre-fame NOFX at their snottiest. 'New Boobs' shouldn't be funny three decades later, and yet.

title: Little Earthquakes
note: Piano and a confession. 'Silent All These Years' is a song that doesn't let you back into the room you were in.

title: Incesticide
note: B-sides and Peel sessions arranged into the best Nirvana record people forget to mention. 'Sliver' is here.

title: Angel Dust
note: The follow-up they could have phoned in, that they sabotaged on purpose instead. Patton at full unhinged.

title: Dirt
note: The heaviest record of the Seattle wave. Layne and Cantrell's harmonies on top of riffs that scrape paint.

title: White Trash, Two Heebs and a Bean
note: Skate punk before skate punk got polite. Still funny, still fast.

title: Singles (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
note: Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Alice in Chains, Mudhoney, Smashing Pumpkins on the same tape, right before MTV made it the story. Cameron Crowe got the snapshot.

title: Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers)
note: Nine voices, dusty kung-fu samples, and a manifesto. Rap rewired.

title: Midnight Marauders
note: Tribe's most consistent, most playable record. Q-Tip and Phife at peak chemistry.

title: In Utero
note: Bleach's noise plus Nevermind's hooks, with Albini on the desk. The honest one.

title: Judgment Night (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
note: The rap-meets-rock crossover album that everyone else spent the '90s trying and failing to replicate. Helmet x House of Pain alone justifies it.

title: The Crow (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
note: The Cure, NIN, Stone Temple Pilots, Pantera, Rage. The compilation that captured the exact mid-90s mood the movie needed.

title: Under the Pink
note: 'Pretty Good Year' and 'Cornflake Girl' on the same record. The mid-period peak.

title: Trashed
note: Melodic skate punk with the tightest rhythm section on Fat Wreck. Cape's voice gives the cynicism a heart.

title: Liquid Swords
note: The most cinematic record in the Wu canon. RZA producing at his murkiest.

title: Only Built 4 Cuban Linx...
note: The purple tape. Mafioso rap's blueprint, Rae and Ghost trading bars like a two-handed novel.

title: Soup
note: The record Shannon Hoon didn't live long enough to defend, and the one that justifies the whole band.

title: On Avery Island
note: Aeroplane's weirder, fuzzier older sibling. The proof Mangum already had the songs before the world noticed.

title: Boys for Pele
note: Recorded in a church in Ireland. The strangest, most unguarded record she's ever made.

title: Endtroducing.....
note: First album built entirely from samples. Cinematic, melancholic, and still feels like the future twenty-five years later.

title: Homogenic
note: Strings and broken beats. The record that proved electronic music could be emotional architecture.

title: In the Aeroplane Over the Sea
note: Lo-fi mysticism. Anne Frank, two-headed boys, and a horn section that sounds like a parade through the afterlife.

title: Mos Def & Talib Kweli Are Black Star
note: Two of the best rappers alive sounding like they just discovered fire. Hi-Tek on the boards.

title: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill
note: One album. That's all she needed. Soul, hip-hop, and a writer's voice that had nobody to compare it to.

title: Mezzanine
note: The dark trip-hop apex. 'Teardrop', 'Angel', 'Inertia Creeps' — pure dread you can move to.

title: Moon Safari
note: French lounge electronica that turned out to be more durable than anyone expected. 'La Femme d'Argent' still parts crowds.

title: The Soft Bulletin
note: Headphones record of the decade. Strings, horns, and the most generous batch of songs Wayne Coyne ever wrote.

title: Summerteeth
note: Sugar on top of dread. Tweedy hiding the darkest lyrics he ever wrote inside the prettiest melodies he ever wrote.

title: The Moon & Antarctica
note: Existential dread you can hum. Isaac Brock's best lyrics by a mile.

title: Kid A
note: The pivot. Guitars traded for static and dread, and somehow more emotional for it. 'How to Disappear Completely' is the floor.

title: Since I Left You
note: Built from thousands of samples and yet sounds like one continuous summer afternoon.

title: Discovery
note: The album that taught a generation what a vocoder was for. Pure joy, on repeat.

title: Vespertine
note: Music boxes, harps, and microbeats. An intimate record played at the volume of an indoor whisper.

title: The Blueprint
note: Kanye's coming-out party as a producer, Just Blaze's golden hour, and Jay sounding untouchable. Released on 9/11 — and the album still ate.

title: White Blood Cells
note: The album that pulled Jack and Meg out of Detroit. Bass-less, drum-light, and somehow louder than everything else on rock radio.

title: Yankee Hotel Foxtrot
note: The sound of a band tearing itself apart on purpose. Static, dread, and 'Jesus, Etc.'

title: Turn On the Bright Lights
note: Post-punk revival distilled. 'NYC' for the city you wished you'd lived in, 'PDA' for the one you did.

title: Yoshimi Battles the Pink Robots
note: Concept record about robots that ends up being about mortality. 'Do You Realize??' earns the question marks.

title: Young Liars
note: The EP that announced them. 'Staring at the Sun' a cappella into doo-wop into static. Nobody else was doing it.

title: Fever to Tell
note: Karen O at her most feral. 'Maps' is the song the rest of the decade tried to write.

title: The Black Album
note: The would-be retirement record. Every producer he ever wanted, and a closing argument for his place at the top.

title: Elephant
note: 'Seven Nation Army' is the floor, not the ceiling. Side B is where the album actually lives.

title: Give Up
note: Ben Gibbard and Jimmy Tamborello mailing tracks to each other. Should've been a one-off; ended up indelible.

title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
note: Before Cookie Mountain hit. The full-length that proved the EP wasn't a fluke.

title: Sung Tongs
note: Two acoustic guitars and a tape machine making a campfire feel haunted.

title: Funeral
note: Grief made anthemic. Every chorus is a snow day with the lights cut.

title: A Ghost Is Born
note: The migraine record. 'At Least That's What You Said' opens with the longest tense pause in rock.

title: Madvillainy
note: Madlib's loops, DOOM's bars. The most quotable, most replayable underground rap record of its decade.

title: MM..FOOD
note: Cereal samples, food bars, and DOOM at his loosest. A breakfast record disguised as a rap album.

title: The Mysterious Production of Eggs
note: Whistling, violin loops, and a vocabulary unlike anyone else writing songs.

title: Illinois
note: Fifty states was always a bit. The Illinoise record was always the point.

title: Apologies to the Queen Mary
note: Two songwriters, two voices, and 'I'll Believe in Anything' — the best closing argument any band ever wrote.

title: Feels
note: The record where AnCo figured out how to write songs without losing the weirdness. 'Grass' alone.

title: Silent Alarm
note: Post-punk angles, jittery drums, and the most caffeinated guitar tones of the decade. 'Like Eating Glass' as opening statement.

title: Return to Cookie Mountain
note: Wolves howling through a wall of guitars. Brooklyn art-rock that earns the term.

title: Show Your Bones
note: The least loved YYYs record and the most rewarding on repeat. 'Cheated Hearts' is the sleeper.

title: Friend and Foe
note: Three guys, a custom-built looping program, and weirder ideas than any of their peers.

title: Let's Stay Friends
note: Tim Harrington in full preacher mode. Brooklyn post-punk with a sense of humor.

title: Sound of Silver
note: 'All My Friends'. 'Someone Great'. 'New York, I Love You But You're Bringing Me Down.' One album, three songs that flatten you.

title: Love Is Simple
note: Communal psych-folk that swerves into chant, into noise, into hymn. A record that sounds like a room full of people.

title: Strawberry Jam
note: The maximalist one. 'Fireworks' and 'Peacebone' make the case for AnCo as pop band, however briefly.

title: Person Pitch
note: Noah Lennox stacking Beach Boys harmonies over loops until they become weather. 'Bros' is twelve minutes that feel like five.

title: Neon Bible
note: Big-room Arcade Fire — pipe organs, Springsteen via Montreal. The dark middle child between Funeral and The Suburbs.

title: Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga
note: Britt Daniel at peak economy. Nothing on the record that doesn't need to be there. 'The Underdog' is a gift.

title: Dear Science
note: Same band, sharper edges, and 'DLZ' for the days that need it.

title: Fleet Foxes
note: Harmonies stacked like cordwood. Robin Pecknold's voice sounded already old when he was 22.

title: Third
note: Eleven-year silence broken by the most paranoid record they ever made. Krautrock pulse under Beth Gibbons's ghost.

title: It's Blitz!
note: The synth pivot worked. 'Zero' is a song that won the back half of the 2000s.

title: Merriweather Post Pavilion
note: Glitchy, sample-heavy, and somehow the most accessible AnCo record. 'My Girls' justified a decade of devotion.

title: This Is Happening
note: Murphy at his most quotable. 'All I Want' is the prettiest song he'll ever write and he knows it.

title: The Suburbs
note: Funeral's grown-up cousin. Cul-de-sacs, bored kids, and the most fully-realized record they'll ever make.

title: Bon Iver
note: Where the cabin-record one-trick guy proved he was a composer. Saxophone solos and town names.

title: Fear Fun
note: Josh Tillman re-introducing himself as a character. Funny, slightly drunk, smarter than it lets on.

title: Run the Jewels 2
note: Killer Mike and El-P at their angriest and best. Hip-hop that earned the late-career renaissance both deserved.

title: I Love You, Honeybear
note: The marriage album. Lush, sarcastic, sincere — sometimes in the same line.

title: DAMN.
note: The Pulitzer record. Front-to-back, back-to-front. The rare album that rewards both modes of listening.

title: IGOR
note: Tyler producing for himself like a different artist. A breakup record disguised as a costume change.

title: Vol. 4
note: The drugs-and-strings record. 'Changes' from the band that invented metal — and the riff factory of 'Snowblind' on the same album.

title: Paul's Boutique
note: The sample-collage masterpiece. Killed commercially on release, vindicated forever after. The Dust Brothers' finest hour.

title: Blind Melon
note: The 'No Rain' record people remember — and the album-deep stuff they forget. 'Change' is the closer that deserved more.

title: Nico
note: The posthumous one. Named for Shannon Hoon's daughter. The version of 'Letters from a Porcupine' is impossible to hear straight.

title: The Score
note: Lauryn, Wyclef, and Pras at the exact moment everything aligned. 'Killing Me Softly' is the floor — the whole record is the ceiling.
Britpop dissolved into William Orbit textures and Damon's heartbreak. 'Tender' is a hymn; 'No Distance Left to Run' is its rebuttal.

title: Good News for People Who Love Bad News
note: The crossover record. 'Float On' was the gateway; the rest of the album is the reason the gateway opened.

title: We Were Dead Before the Ship Even Sank
note: Johnny Marr joined the band, and the songs got bigger. Sea-shanty rhythms behind Isaac Brock's best dread.

title: Face Control
note: Dan Boeckner and Alexei Perry making airport-bar synth-punk. The political record dressed up as a dance record.

title: Sound Kapital
note: Their farewell, recorded around tours of Beijing and Myanmar. Synths and shouting — what would have been their best record had they kept going.

title: Check Your Head
note: The instruments-back-in-our-hands record. Punk-rap-funk-hardcore in one stew, and the band most able to pull it off.

title: 2014 Forest Hills Drive
note: No features. Self-produced. The grown-up record made by an artist who knew exactly what he wanted to say.

title: Jar of Flies
note: The first EP to debut at #1. Acoustic, melancholy, and the most emotionally direct thing the band ever recorded.

title: Ill Communication
note: Funk, hardcore, rap, and 'Sabotage' as the moment a music video changed the band's career arc.

title: Tical
note: First Wu solo. RZA's grimiest beats, Meth's voice already iconic. The album that proved the Wu strategy worked.

title: MTV Unplugged in New York
note: Released after Cobain died. The cover of 'Where Did You Sleep Last Night' is the band's last word.

title: MTV Unplugged
note: Their last full show with Layne. The performance is fragile, beautiful, and impossible to hear without weight.

title: Blazing Arrow
note: Gift of Gab's tongue-twisting verses over Chief Xcel's warm soul samples. The most listenable backpack rap record of its era.

title: Supreme Clientele
note: Wu's most quotable solo record. Bars that don't always make sense and yet always make sense. RZA back on form.

title: Remain in Light
note: Byrne, Eno, and a rhythm section possessed by Fela. The album that proved a new-wave band could become a polyrhythmic religion.

title: Holy Diver
note: Ronnie James Dio's solo debut. The cover, the title track, and 'Rainbow in the Dark' as a one-two-three for the heavy-metal high school years.

title: Sacred Heart
note: More fantasy, more bombast. 'Rock 'n' Roll Children' is the song you remember; the rest of the record rewards you for staying.

title: Vulgar Display of Power
note: Where groove metal finally won. Dimebag's riffs are still the textbook. Phil Anselmo's bark made everyone else sound polite.

title: Far Beyond Driven
note: Debuted at #1 with no radio play. The angriest, most punishing record on the major-label charts that year, by a wide margin.

title: Speaking in Tongues
note: Post-Eno, leaner, and the pop record nobody saw coming. 'Burning Down the House' is the floor.

title: Graceland
note: Ladysmith Black Mambazo, mbaqanga rhythms, and a songwriter at the height of his curiosity. The cultural-exchange record that earned every defender.

title: Rage Against the Machine
note: Politics and riffs, with nothing between them. Morello's tone alone made guitar an argument again.

title: Pretty Hate Machine
note: Reznor alone in a Cleveland studio inventing industrial pop. 'Head Like a Hole' was the warning shot.

title: Broken
note: The angriest record Reznor ever made, recorded while trapped in a label contract. Six tracks of pure exit-wound rage.

title: Opiate
note: The first EP. Six tracks, no patience for polish. The most punk thing they ever released.

title: Undertow
note: Before they got prog. Heaviest, most direct Tool record. 'Sober' and 'Prison Sex' as a one-two argument.

title: Ænima
note: The pivot to prog. 'Stinkfist', 'Forty Six & 2', and 'Eulogy' as a thesis statement. The record that defined the rest of their career.

title: Add It Up (1981-1993)
note: Not strictly an album — a compilation that functions as one. Gano's catalogue compressed into its sharpest, most playable form.
